children.text: The Hofileña Ancestral House was built in 1934 and has been open to the public since 1962, the first heritage house in Silay to welcome visitors. It displays more than 1,000 works, including pieces by Juan Luna and Amorsolo, along with antiques. Visitors tour it with a guide who tells the story of life and taste during the Negros sugar boom.
The Hofileña Ancestral House is a lifestyle museum on Cinco de Noviembre Street in Silay City, Negros Occidental. Manuel Severino Hofileña built it in
for his wife, Gilda Ledesma Hojilla (said to have been a former Miss Silay), and their nine children. It is still the Hofileña family home as well as an exhibition space. It opened to the public in
and is recorded as the first ancestral house in Silay to do so.

The building takes the traditional Filipino bahay na bato form and layers 1930s Art Deco and Art Nouveau influences and American elements over it. The eaves are deep and wide, and the broad steps up to the entrance are described as showing American influence. The main materials are hardwoods: narra for the floors, balayong (an ironwood) for the walls, and callado, an openwork carved tracery, in the doors. The grand balayong staircase in the middle of the house was moved from Gilda Hofileña's family home, and every baluster was carved by hand.

What makes this house special is less the building than what is inside it. The second-floor gallery holds more than 1,000 works of art, including pieces by leading Filipino masters such as Juan Luna, Félix Resurrección Hidalgo, Fernando Amorsolo, Ang Kiukok, Vicente Manansala, Hernando Ocampo and BenCab. A sketch said to be by José Rizal and a painting attributed to Francisco Goya are also presented as part of the collection. The sala, library, dining room and bedroom hold collectibles such as a 200-year-old German piano, Ming dynasty jars and an Israeli oil juglet said to be about 3,000 years old.

The real pleasure of a visit is the guided tour. Many visitors report that for years a member of the family personally welcomed guests and told stories about the paintings, the family, the sugar boom years and Negros culture. Heading north from Bacolod, the house pairs well with the rest of Silay's heritage street, including Balay Negrense and the Bernardino Jalandoni Museum, for a half-day route.

This is the heart of the house, with more than 1,000 works on display. Names mentioned include Juan Luna, Hidalgo, Amorsolo, Ang Kiukok, Manansala, Ocampo and BenCab, and some visitors report seeing paintings by Conrado Judith, a self-taught Silay artist. For security reasons, access to the second floor may be limited or photography may be banned, so follow the staff's instructions.

This is a 1930s wooden mansion with narra floors, balayong walls and callado tracery in the doors. The deep eaves and wide entrance steps are explained as American influence, and an Art Deco and Art Nouveau mood mixes with the bahay na bato style.

The large staircase at the center of the house was moved from Gilda Hofileña's family home, and each baluster was carved by hand. It is often mentioned in introductions to Negros heritage, so many visitors want a photo, but check on site which areas you may photograph.

blocks.title: Collectibles in the sala and library

children.text: The sala has family photographs, a roughly 200-year-old German Steinweg piano, Spanish chairs and a hand-carved kamagong sofa. The library holds Filipiniana books, pocketbooks issued to American soldiers in World War II, and a wooden image of Saint Vincent Ferrer.

Cabinets hold toys collected on travels, dolls described as smaller than a grain of rice, and tektite stones. The owner's tastes show everywhere, so it feels more like looking around a lived-in home than a museum.

blocks.title: Porcelain and the first wood-printing press in the dining room

children.text: The dining room (comedor) has Chinese porcelain, Ming dynasty jars and an Israeli oil juglet said to be about 3,000 years old, and it also displays the first wood-printing press used in Negros. The press is said to be demonstrated occasionally.

blocks.title: A record of war and an art theft

children.text: During World War II the family is said to have fled to the mountains, Japanese commanders held meetings in the house, and Americans stayed there afterward. In
July 2024
Amorsolo's 1936 painting "Mango Harvesters" was stolen, then recovered by the NBI and returned to the museum in
April 2025
. For that reason, second-floor viewing rules are now strict.

blocks.title: NHCP historical marker and a setting for film and TV

children.text: The National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) installed a historical marker on
April 6, 1993
. The BBC program "Far Eastern Cookery" filmed here in
, and in 2011 a Canadian documentary on the Negros sugar industry used the house as a setting.

items.title: Silay half-day route
items.subtitle: Three heritage houses starting from Bacolod

children.text: Leave Bacolod for Silay to the north. A car or taxi is the easiest way, and by public transport you take a bus from the Bacolod North Terminal toward Victorias and get off in Silay. Confirm the exact fare when you board.
After arriving in Silay, first walk around San Diego Pro-Cathedral, then head toward Cinco de Noviembre Street. The houses are close together, so alternating walking and tricycle rides works well.

Arrive at the Hofileña Ancestral House and ring the entrance bell to ask for a guide. On the ground floor you tour the sala, library, dining room and bedroom with the guide, and you see the second-floor gallery to the extent it is allowed. Allow about
1 hour
Have lunch at a nearby cafe or restaurant. Visitors report cafes in Silay set in old mansions, so check on site that they are open and what hours they keep.
Visit Balay Negrense and the Bernardino Jalandoni Museum (the Pink House). Balay Negrense may be closed for restoration, so check the latest announcement before you go.
Return to Bacolod and have dinner at a seaside restaurant as the sun sets, or carry on with your city plans.
Opening days and hours differ from house to house. Many are said to close on Mondays, so it is safest to avoid Monday.
Domestic flights run from Manila to Bacolod-Silay Airport (BCD). Carriers and times change by season, so check with the airline.
The airport lies within Silay, close to the heritage district. An older report put a tricycle from the airport to downtown Silay at about
, but the fare is often higher now, so negotiate on the spot.
You could also reach Negros from Manila via Cebu and a ferry, but it takes long, so a direct flight is easier for most travelers.
Take a bus bound for Victorias from the Bacolod North Terminal and get off in Silay. In older reports the fare was around
, and it may be higher now.
By taxi or ride-hailing car the trip usually takes about
30 minutes to 1 hour
, depending on traffic.
Some tour packages offer a Silay heritage tour with hotel pickup in Bacolod. Prices vary by operator.
The houses along Cinco de Noviembre Street are within walking distance of one another.
When it is hot, use a tricycle or pedicab. Agree on the destination and fare before you get in.
Visitors with cars are told there is parking inside the grounds, but check the situation on site.
Since the visit is mostly indoors, rain will not ruin your plans, but if you want to walk between several houses, the dry season of
December–May
is more comfortable. One account says guides run tours around Negros Occidental in December, so the year-end season can bring more visitors.
Bacolod's MassKara Festival takes place in
October
and the whole city gets crowded. Book lodging and transport in advance for that period. Visitors say Silay is relatively quiet on weekday afternoons.

Most people visit Silay as a day trip and book their lodging in Bacolod. Bacolod has a wide choice of hotels, and its downtown restaurants and seaside seafood places are close by, which makes it a good spot for dinner after the house tour.

Visitors report cafes and restaurants in Silay that make use of old mansions, and the long-established bakery El Ideal is often mentioned. Hours and menus can change, so check on the day. In Bacolod, the Negros specialty chicken inasal and sweet desserts are famous.
There may be no large sign at the entrance. Look for the small museum sign and doorbell, and ring it to ask for a guide.
Photography is allowed in many places on the ground floor, but the second-floor gallery is either off-limits for photos or has restricted access. Ask first, then shoot.
Listening to the guide makes it easier to understand the context of the collection. Asking questions and offering a tip is good manners.
Many heritage houses are said to close on Mondays, so check your day of visit.
Rather than staying long at one place, plan a half day that combines Balay Negrense, the Pink House and the cathedral.
It is hot at midday in the dry season. Bring a hat, water and sunscreen, and do most of your walking in the morning.
Admission and opening hours differ by source and are hard to confirm. Check local announcements and social media before you go.
Admission has been reported anywhere from ₱50 to ₱150, depending on the account. Check the latest announcement.
After the 2024 theft, rules on second-floor access and photography may have been tightened. Follow the staff's directions.
Other Silay heritage houses, such as Balay Negrense, may be closed for restoration, which could throw your schedule off.
This is an old wooden building, so watch your step on the stairs and floors to avoid slipping, and do not touch the exhibits.
It is also the Hofileña family's home, so keep your voice down and avoid unreasonable requests.
Known as the "Paris of Negros," this heritage city gathers ancestral house museums, a cathedral and sweet shops. You can see
Silay
on foot across the whole town center.
This cathedral in the center of Silay is close to the heritage district and fits naturally into a walking route.
These are the ruins of a sugar baron's mansion on the Talisay side, and many travelers combine them with a Bacolod and Silay itinerary. It is roughly
10 km
away, so check how you will get there.
The central city of Negros Occidental, with lodging, restaurants and downtown sights. It lies to the south of Silay.
